quote: when he took less risk than any of the people marching with him
content: As a claim about Gandhi's whole life, "less risk than any" is false. The Durban mob, the 1908 beating and the assassination are all real, and the lifetime comparison should be dropped. The essay's comparison is within a march, and there the record matches its picture. At the Dharasana Salt Works in May 1930, Gandhi was already in custody, arrested days before, while column after column of anonymous satyagrahis walked up to the police lines and were clubbed down. Webb Miller's dispatch describing it went around the world. The celebrity was taken into detention and the unnamed were taken to hospital. That is the essay's anonymous marcher who "walked with a limp for the rest of her life," and Fable concedes this "grain of truth" is the essay's actual point.

quote: “Whoever saves a single life, it is as if he had saved the whole world” may be a fine applause light, but it’s terrible moral advice if you’ve got to pick one or the other.
content: The Mishnah's context is conceded: it is the admonition to witnesses in capital cases. The essay's sentence is conditional, though: "terrible moral advice if you've got to pick one or the other." It is aimed at the saying's modern use as a free-floating applause line, where it stands in for arithmetic in exactly the cases that call for triage, as in a charity appeal or the closing of a film. Fable's own reading makes the two compatible: "one life is of incalculable weight" and "save two hundred rather than three" answer different questions. That is the essay's analysis. It asks which question the saying answers and grants it the one it does. What it objects to is using the saying for the other.
